summary: Specifies version 2 of the Network Time Protocol, which synchronizes clocks and distributes time across a large internet. It describes the formal structure and gives implementation information. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1305.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers each have their own clock and they drift apart. This is a way for them to ask each other the time and all agree.

subtitle: Synchronizing clocks across a distributed internet of diverse networks and time servers

tldr.problem: Computers on the internet have clocks that drift at different rates, making it impossible for them to coordinate events or measure delays accurately without a common time.
tldr.mechanism: NTP version 2 organizes time servers into a hierarchical stratum system, where servers at each level synchronize with servers at lower strata (closer to primary reference sources like radio clocks). Peers exchange timestamped messages, measure roundtrip delay and clock offset, filter out bad samples, and adjust their local oscillators.
tldr.outcome: NTP allows computers across the internet to synchronize their clocks to within milliseconds of each other and of UTC, even when faced with long, variable network delays and occasional failures.

today: RFC 1119 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 1305 (NTP version 3). NTP version 4 and later versions continue to evolve, but the hierarchical stratum concept and the core synchronization algorithms described here remain central to how the internet keeps time.

sections.title: Purpose and Design
sections.content: The Network Time Protocol (NTP) version 2 synchronizes time and distributes time across a large internet. It specifies architectures, algorithms, entities and protocols for maintaining accuracy and robustness even over paths with long, variable delays. NTP uses a self-organizing, hierarchical-master-slave configuration with synchronization paths determined by a minimum-weight spanning tree. Multiple primary servers may exist at the root, but no election protocol is required.
sections.plainLanguage: NTP lets computers ask multiple time servers for the time and automatically pick the best answer, even when network delays are long and variable.

sections.title: Stratum and Modes
sections.content: NTP organizes time servers into strata: stratum 1 servers are directly connected to a primary reference source (a radio clock locked to UTC), stratum 2 servers synchronize from stratum 1, and so on. The synchronization subnet automatically reconfigures itself into a hierarchical structure minimizing distance to the root. NTP can operate in five modes: symmetric active and passive (peers synchronize each other), client/server (workstations request time from servers), and broadcast (servers push time to many clients on a LAN). Each mode specifies how associations are created, maintained and dissolved.
sections.plainLanguage: A primary time server listens to a radio clock. Secondary servers ask the primary. Clients ask the secondaries. Everyone organizes themselves into the best hierarchy.

sections.title: Measurement and Filtering
sections.content: When two hosts exchange NTP messages, each host records four timestamps: when it sent the message, when the peer received it, when the peer sent its reply, and when the host received the reply. From these four times, NTP computes the roundtrip delay (the time the message took to travel both ways) and the clock offset (how much ahead or behind the peer this host is). NTP collects multiple samples from each peer, filters them to remove outliers and jitter, and selects a single trusted peer as its primary time source based on accuracy, reliability and stratum level.
sections.plainLanguage: Each computer sends a time request with a timestamp and the server responds with its own timestamps. The computers use these four timestamps to measure both the delay and the time difference.

sections.title: Precision and Implementation
sections.content: NTP timestamps are 64-bit numbers representing seconds since January 1, 1900, with the first 32 bits as the integer part and the last 32 bits as a fractional part, giving a precision of about 200 picoseconds. The RFC specifies standard parameters: UDP port 123, maximum stratum of 15, maximum polling interval of 1024 seconds (about 17 minutes), and minimum polling interval of 64 seconds. The RFC includes detailed algorithms for local-clock adjustment, oscillator stability considerations, and recommendations for handling leap seconds inserted into UTC.
sections.plainLanguage: NTP uses a special timestamp format accurate to billionths of a second. Computers can ask for time as often as every 64 seconds or as rarely as every 17 minutes, depending on network stability.
